claim: Apical secretion from epithelial tubes of the Drosophila embryo is mediated by apical F-actin cables generated by the formin-family protein Diaphanous (Dia).
source: Apical secretion from epithelial tubes of the Drosophila embryo is mediated by apical F-actin cables generated by the formin-family protein Diaphanous (Dia).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Massarwa et al., 2009) and represents established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 levels at the apical membrane regulate Dia localization in both the MDCK cyst model and in Drosophila tubular epithelia.
source: PI(4,5)P2 levels at the apical membrane regulate Dia localization in both the MDCK cyst model and in Drosophila tubular epithelia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3, 4, and 5 showing manipulations of PI(4,5)P2 levels and their effects on Dia localization.

claim: An N-terminal basic domain of Dia is crucial for apical localization, implying direct binding to PI(4,5)P2.
source: An N-terminal basic domain of Dia is crucial for apical localization, implying direct binding to PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing that deletion of the basic domain reduces apical localization, and by inference from the known electrostatic binding properties of basic domains to acidic phospholipids.

claim: Dia apical targeting depends on binding to Rho1, which is critical for activation-induced conformational change and physically anchoring Dia to the apical membrane.
source: Dia apical targeting also depends on binding to Rho1, which is critical for activation-induced conformational change, as well as physically anchoring Dia to the apical membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing effects of Rho1 depletion and mutations in the Rho1-binding domain on Dia localization.

claim: Binding to Rho1 facilitates interaction with PI(4,5)P2 at the plane of the membrane.
source: We demonstrate that binding to Rho1 facilitates interaction with PI(4,5)P2 at the plane of the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing synergistic effects of Rho1 and PI(4,5)P2 binding on Dia localization (Figure 7), and by inference from the observation that the basic domain alone is insufficient for localization.

claim: Endogenous Dia exhibits a highly polarized distribution, accumulating at the apical surface of epithelial cells in diverse tubular tissues of the Drosophila embryo.
source: Endogenous Dia exhibits a highly polarized distribution, accumulating at the apical surface of epithelial cells in diverse tubular tissues of the Drosophila embryo (Figure 1A–C; Massarwa et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A-C and by citation to previous work.

claim: A full-length Dia construct (GFP-Dia-FL) displayed an apically polarized distribution, albeit less dramatic than the endogenous protein.
source: Upon expression at similar levels to endogenous Dia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), a full-length Dia construct (GFP-Dia-FL) displayed an apically polarized distribution, albeit less dramatic than the endogenous protein (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 1D-F and quantification in Figure 1J-L.

claim: GFP-Dia-ΔDAD displays a much tighter apical localization pattern than GFP-Dia-FL.
source: While expression of this construct in tubular epithelia results in protein levels similar to the full-length form (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), GFP-Dia-ΔDAD displays a much tighter apical localization pattern (Figure 1G–I), suggesting that the molecule is now more accessible to apical-targeting signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 1G-I and quantification showing up to fourfold enhancement in apical enrichment.

claim: Apical enrichment of GFP-Dia-ΔDAD is enhanced up to fourfold relative to GFP-Dia-FL.
source: Quantification demonstrates that apical enrichment of GFP-Dia-ΔDAD is enhanced up to fourfold relative to GFP-Dia-FL (Figure 1J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Approximately 45% of the total GFP intensity in GFP-Dia-ΔDAD expressing cells is concentrated at the apical surface, which encompasses only approximately 5% of the total cell area.
source: Further measurements in GFP-Dia-ΔDAD expressing cells reveal that ∼45% of the total GFP intensity in the cell is concentrated at the apical surface, which encompasses only ∼5% of the total cell area.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of fluorescence intensity distribution in cells.

claim: A construct containing only the C-terminal half of Dia (GFP-Dia-C′) was distributed within the cytoplasm upon expression in tubular epithelia.
source: A construct containing only the C-terminal half (GFP-Dia-C′) was distributed within the cytoplasm upon expression in tubular epithelia (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal construct (GFP-Dia-N′) displayed striking apical enrichment, reminiscent of the localization pattern of the intact GFP-Dia-ΔDAD open molecule.
source: In contrast, the reciprocal N-terminal construct (GFP-Dia-N′) displayed striking apical enrichment, reminiscent of the localization pattern of the intact GFP-Dia-ΔDAD open molecule (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal half of Dia is both necessary and sufficient for apical targeting.
source: These observations suggest that the N-terminal half of Dia is both necessary and sufficient for apical targeting.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that GFP-Dia-N′ localizes apically while GFP-Dia-C′ does not.

claim: When the dimerization domain (DD) was added to the Dia-C′ construct (GFP-Dia-DD-C′), no apical localization was detected.
source: However, when the dimerization domain (DD) was added to the Dia-C′ construct (GFP-Dia-DD-C′), no apical localization was detected (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that apical localization of Dia constructs is not biased by dimerization to endogenous Dia.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 2D-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The open conformation of Dia facilitates efficient apical localization by exposing critical domains to targeting cues.
source: Taken together, this structure–function analysis supports a model whereby the open conformation of Dia facilitates efficient apical localization by exposing critical domains to targeting cues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations that the open form (ΔDAD) shows enhanced apical localization compared to the full-length form.

claim: The Dia-targeting regions are restricted to the N-terminal half of the protein.
source: The Dia-targeting regions are restricted to the N-terminal half of the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that the N-terminal construct localizes apically while the C-terminal construct does not.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is a key determinant of the apical membrane in 3D cysts of cultured MDCK cells, where it is highly enriched.
source: In 3D cysts of cultured Madin–Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells, a well-established system for recapitulation of epithelial tube morphogenesis, PI(4,5)P2 is a key determinant of the apical membrane, where it is highly enriched (Martin-Belmonte et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Drosophila GFP-Dia-FL failed to localize to a specific subcellular domain, and was homogenously distributed in the cytoplasm of MDCK cyst cells.
source: Drosophila GFP-Dia-FL failed to localize to a specific subcellular domain, and was homogenously distributed in the cytoplasm of cyst cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 3A.

claim: Drosophila GFP-Dia-ΔDAD was targeted apically in MDCK cysts, co-localizing with the apical marker gp-135.
source: In marked contrast, Drosophila GFP-Dia-ΔDAD was targeted apically, co-localizing with the apical marker gp-135 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 3B showing colocalization with gp-135.

claim: Exogenous PI(4,5)P2 delivery to the basal surface of MDCK cysts expressing GFP-Dia-ΔDAD caused redistribution from the apical to the basal surface within 10 minutes.
source: GFP-Dia-ΔDAD localization was dramatically altered, even after very short treatments of 10 min, displaying redistribution from the apical to the basal surface, while remaining apical in mock treated cysts (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 3C-F showing the redistribution of GFP-Dia-ΔDAD following PI(4,5)P2 treatment.

claim: The rapid shift in GFP-Dia-ΔDAD localization preceded the general shift in polarity induced by exogenous PI(4,5)P2 treatment in MDCK cysts.
source: The rapid shift in GFP-Dia-ΔDAD localization preceded the general shift in polarity induced by exogenous PI(4,5)P2 treatment in this system (Martin-Belmonte et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous work and by observation that the apical marker gp-135 remained partially apical while Dia redistributed.

claim: The rapid nature of Dia re-localization suggests that recruitment to the baso-lateral membranes is a direct result of exogenous PI(4,5)P2 treatment.
source: The rapid nature of Dia re-localization suggests that recruitment to the baso-lateral membranes is a direct result of exogenous PI(4,5)P2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that redistribution occurs within 10 minutes, before general polarity changes.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 could fulfill a prominent role in the regulation of Dia apical targeting in tubular structures.
source: These observations imply that PI(4,5)P2 could fulfill a prominent role in the regulation of Dia apical targeting in tubular structures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the MDCK cyst experiments showing PI(4,5)P2-dependent Dia localization.

claim: PH-PLCδ-GFP, a PI(4,5)P2 sensor, showed significant apical enrichment in the embryonic hindgut and larval salivary gland cells.
source: Imaging the GFP fluorescence in live tissues showed significant apical enrichment of the sensor in the embryonic hindgut and larval salivary gland cells (Figure 4B,D), which was apparent but less pronounced in the embryonic trachea (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Apical membranes of Drosophila tubular epithelia are enriched in PI(4,5)P2, as in mammalian systems.
source: Apical membranes of Drosophila tubular epithelia are therefore enriched in PI(4,5)P2, as in mammalian systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by the PI(4,5)P2 sensor data and by comparison with known mammalian systems.

claim: Skittles (Sktl), one of the two Drosophila PIP5-kinases which catalyze PI(4,5)P2 production from PI(4)P, was shown to be critical for PI(4,5)P2 production in various systems.
source: Skittles (Sktl), one of the two Drosophila PIP5-kinases which catalyze PI(4,5)P2 production from PI(4)P (Figure 4A), was shown to be critical for PI(4,5)P2 production in various systems (Gervais et al., 2008; Fabian et al., 2010), and is endogenously expressed in different Drosophila embryonic tubular organs (BDGP-Berkeley Drosophila Genome Project).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and reference to expression database.

claim: An RFP-tagged version of Sktl was targeted predominantly to the apical surface of tubular organ cells.
source: Indeed, when we expressed an RFP-tagged version of Sktl in Drosophila tubular organs, it was targeted predominantly to the apical surface of cells (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Apical targeting of Sktl may account for PI(4,5)P2 accumulation at the apical membrane.
source: Thus, apical targeting of Sktl may account for PI(4,5)P2 accumulation at this membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Sktl, which produces PI(4,5)P2, is apically localized.

claim: A mutated form of Sktl with an inactive kinase domain (Sktl-KID) was no longer enriched apically, and instead assumed a general cortical distribution.
source: We find a similar relationship in Drosophila tubular organs between Sktl activity and apical localization: a mutated form of Sktl, where the kinase domain is inactive (Sktl-KID), was no longer enriched apically, and instead assumed a general cortical distribution (Figure 4H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 4H-J.

claim: Apically-biased Sktl generates PI(4,5)P2 at the apical membrane of tubular organs, and elevated apical PI(4,5)P2 serves to reinforce apical targeting of Sktl.
source: Taken together, these observations are consistent with a scenario where apically-biased Sktl generates PI(4,5)P2 at the apical membrane of tubular organs. Elevated apical PI(4,5)P2 then serves to reinforce apical targeting of Sktl, and provides an apical cue for additional proteins such as Dia.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations that Sktl localizes apically, produces PI(4,5)P2, and that the kinase-dead form loses apical localization.

claim: The partial apical localization of GFP-Dia-FL in tracheal cells is significantly enhanced upon co-expression with Sktl-RFP.
source: The partial apical localization of GFP-Dia-FL in tracheal cells (Figures 1D and 5A) is barely detectable at late embryonic stages (Figure 5C), but is significantly enhanced upon co-expression with Sktl-RFP (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5A-D and quantification in Figure 5G.

claim: Apical enrichment of GFP-Dia-FL was not observed following co-expression of Sktl with the GFP-Dia-C′ construct, which does not contain apical targeting activity.
source: Conversely, apical enrichment was not observed following co-expression of Sktl with the GFP-Dia-C′ construct, which does not contain apical targeting activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5E.

claim: GFP-Dia-FL localization was not affected by co-expression with the catalytically inactive form of Sktl.
source: Moreover, GFP-Dia-FL localization was not affected by co-expression with the catalytically inactive form of Sktl (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5F.

claim: Sktl-dependent increase in PI(4,5)P2 levels at the apical membrane leads to enhanced recruitment of Dia.
source: These results suggest that Sktl-dependent increase in PI(4,5)P2 levels at the apical membrane leads to enhanced recruitment of Dia.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experiments showing that Sktl overexpression enhances Dia apical localization, but only when Sktl is catalytically active.

claim: PTEN dephosphorylates PI(3,4,5)P3 to form PI(4,5)P2, thus acting as a negative regulator of the PI3K pathway.
source: An additional regulator of PI(4,5)P2 levels in the membrane is the lipid phosphatase PTEN, which dephosphorylates PI(3,4,5)P3 to form PI(4,5)P2, thus acting as a negative regulator of the PI3K pathway (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim represents established biochemical knowledge about PTEN function.

claim: PTEN has been shown to be associated with the regulation of cell polarity in both Drosophila and mammalian systems.
source: PTEN has been shown to be associated with the regulation of cell polarity in both Drosophila and mammalian systems (Martin-Belmonte et al., 2007; Chartier et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PTEN resides at adherens junctions, consistent with a role in the maintenance of PI(4,5)P2 levels at the apical membrane.
source: PTEN resides at adherens junctions (von Stein et al., 2005), consistent with a role in the maintenance of PI(4,5)P2 levels at the apical membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and inference about its functional role.

claim: The PI(4,5)P2 sensor PH-PLCδ-GFP is localized apically in larval salivary glands.
source: The PI(4,5)P2 sensor PH-PLCδ-GFP is localized apically in larval salivary glands, similar to other tubular organs (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H.

claim: A pronounced redistribution of the PI(4,5)P2 sensor was observed following co-expression of Pten-RNAi, such that the sensor became evenly localized around the cortex of salivary-gland cells.
source: A pronounced redistribution of the sensor was observed following co-expression of Pten-RNAi, such that the sensor became evenly localized around the cortex of salivary-gland cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5I.

claim: Expression of a Pten-RNAi construct caused a dramatic redistribution of the GFP-Dia-N′ construct, from a restricted apical localization to a homogenous distribution throughout the plasma membrane of third instar salivary gland cells.
source: Similar to the effect on the PI(4,5)P2 sensor localization pattern, expression of a Pten-RNAi construct caused a dramatic redistribution of the GFP-Dia-N′ construct, from a restricted apical localization to a homogenous distribution throughout the plasma membrane of third instar salivary gland cells (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5J-K.

claim: The localization of the CD8-RFP construct remained apically restricted following Pten knockdown, indicating that the loss of PTEN specifically affected Dia localization.
source: The localization of the CD8-RFP construct remained apically restricted following Pten knockdown, indicating that the loss of PTEN specifically affected Dia localization (Figure 5J″–K″).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5J″-K″ showing that CD8-RFP remains apical while Dia redistributes.

claim: Manipulations of PI(4,5)P2 levels profoundly and specifically affect Dia localization in vivo, demonstrating the involvement of PI(4,5)P2 in Dia apical targeting.
source: In summary, manipulations of PI(4,5)P2 levels profoundly and specifically affect Dia localization in vivo, demonstrating the involvement of PI(4,5)P2 in Dia apical targeting.
evidence: This claim summarizes the experimental findings from Sktl overexpression and PTEN knockdown experiments.

claim: The mammalian homologues of Dia, mDia1 and mDia2, directly bind acidic phospholipids via electrostatic interactions, involving basic stretches near the N-terminus of the protein, termed the Basic Domain (BD).
source: Previous reports showed that the mammalian homologues of Dia, mDia1 and mDia2, directly bind acidic phospholipids via electrostatic interactions, involving basic stretches near the N-terminus of the protein, termed the Basic Domain (BD) (Ramalingam et al., 2010; Gorelik et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Drosophila Dia N-terminal 60 amino acids are enriched for basic residues.
source: Indeed the Drosophila Dia N-terminal 60 amino acids are also enriched for basic residues (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Deletion of the BD profoundly reduced apical targeting of the GFP-Dia-N′ reporter in larval salivary glands, as well as in other tubular tissues.
source: Deletion of the BD profoundly reduced apical targeting of the GFP-Dia-N′ reporter in larval salivary glands, as well as in other tubular tissues (Figure 6A–B, 7G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), demonstrating its significance for Dia localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6A-B, Figure 7G, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: No apical localization bias was observed for the GFP-Dia-BD construct, as confirmed by comparison to the localization of GFP alone.
source: Remarkably, no apical localization bias was observed for this protein, as was also confirmed by comparison to the localization of GFP alone, and measurements of GFP apical enrichment (Figure 6C–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6C-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Despite being critical for Dia localization, the basic domain is not sufficient on its own to drive apical targeting.
source: Thus, despite being critical for Dia localization, the basic domain is not sufficient on its own to drive apical targeting.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations that deletion of BD reduces localization but BD alone does not localize apically.

claim: A GFP-Rho1 construct specifically expressed in third instar larval salivary gland cells showed clear enrichment at the apical surface.
source: An initial indication that Rho1 can serve as an apical recruitment factor for Dia came from examination of Rho1 protein localization. A GFP-Rho1 construct specifically expressed in third instar larval salivary gland cells showed clear enrichment at the apical surface (Figure 7A), as did a GFP fusion protein expressed from the endogenous Rho1 promoter (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7A.

claim: Apical enrichment of GFP-Rho1 was not altered upon co-expression with a dia-RNAi construct, indicating that it is not mediated by Dia protein or by actin structures generated by Dia.
source: Apical enrichment of GFP-Rho1 was not altered upon co-expression with a dia-RNAi construct, indicating that it is not mediated by Dia protein or by actin structures generated by Dia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP-Dia-N′ localization was dramatically altered upon co-expression with a Rho1–RNAi construct, and displayed a uniform distribution in the cytoplasm.
source: GFP-Dia-N′ localization was dramatically altered upon co-expression with a Rho1–RNAi construct, and displayed a uniform distribution in the cytoplasm (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7B-C.

claim: GFP-Dia-N′-mutG, a GFP-Dia-N′ variant mutated at residues that confer Rho1 binding, displayed an essentially cytoplasmic distribution upon expression in larval salivary glands and various embryonic tubular tissues.
source: Furthermore, a similar outcome was obtained following expression of GFP-Dia-N′-mutG (Figure 2A), a GFP-Dia-N′ variant, which is mutated at residues that confer Rho1 binding (Otomo et al., 2005; Rose et al., 2005; Lammers et al., 2008). The distribution of GFP-Dia-N′-mutG was essentially cytoplasmic upon expression in larval salivary glands, as well as in various embryonic tubular tissues (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2), indicating that direct interaction with Rho1 mediates Dia targeting.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Direct interaction with Rho1 mediates Dia targeting.
source: The distribution of GFP-Dia-N′-mutG was essentially cytoplasmic upon expression in larval salivary glands, as well as in various embryonic tubular tissues (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2), indicating that direct interaction with Rho1 mediates Dia targeting.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mutation of the Rho1-binding domain abolishes apical localization.

claim: Apically-localized Rho1 functions to physically anchor Dia to the apical surface, in addition to opening the protein.
source: Thus, apically-localized Rho1 functions to physically anchor Dia to the apical surface, in addition to opening the protein.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experiments showing that the open form of Dia (Dia-N′) still requires Rho1 for apical localization.

claim: Rho1 exerts both activation and anchoring activities only in the active, GTP-bound form.
source: We assume that Rho1 exerts both activities only in the active, GTP-bound form (Rose et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to previous work and represents an assumption based on known Rho1 biology.

claim: Rho1 localization was not altered following different manipulations designed to modify PI(4,5)P2 levels, including Sktl over-expression and PTEN depletion.
source: First, Rho1 localization was not altered following different manipulations designed to modify PI(4,5)P2 levels and affect Dia localization, including Sktl over-expression and PTEN depletion (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The PI(4,5)P2 reporter PH-PLCδ-GFP remained apically enriched following co-expression with a Rho1–RNAi construct, indicating that Rho1 does not directly regulate PI(4,5)P2 distribution.
source: Similarly, when we monitored the PI(4,5)P2 reporter PH-PLCδ-GFP, it remained apically enriched following co-expression with a Rho1–RNAi construct (Figure 7—figure supplement 3), indicating that Rho1 does not directly regulate PI(4,5)P2 distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Co-expression of GFP-Dia-N′ΔBD with Rho1-RNAi or expression of a GFP-Dia-N′ΔBD mutG construct resulted in complete loss of apical localization.
source: Co-expression of GFP-Dia-N′ΔBD with Rho1-RNAi or expression of a GFP-Dia-N′ΔBD mutG construct resulted in complete loss of apical localization (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7E-G.

claim: The residual apical localization observed for the GFP-Dia-N′ΔBD construct can be attributed to Rho1 binding.
source: This indicates that the residual apical localization observed for the GFP-Dia-N′ΔBD construct (Figure 6B) can be attributed to Rho1 binding, consistent with the notion of two distinct functional modules for Dia binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that removing Rho1 binding eliminates the residual localization of the BD-deleted construct.

claim: The inability of the BD to direct even a mild bias of apical localization on its own suggests that the Dia–PI(4,5)P2 interaction requires simultaneous binding of an apical cue through an additional domain.
source: However, the inability of the BD to direct even a mild bias of apical localization on its own (Figure 6C), suggests that the Dia–PI(4,5)P2 interaction requires simultaneous binding of an apical cue through an additional domain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that BD alone does not localize apically despite being necessary for localization.

claim: While the capacity to bind PI(4,5)P2 does not promote apical localization in the absence of Rho1, it strongly enhances apical targeting of Dia when Rho1 is present.
source: While the capacity to bind PI(4,5)P2 does not promote apical localization in the absence of Rho1, it strongly enhances apical targeting of Dia when Rho1 is present (Figure 7G, compare Dia-N′ΔBD with Dia-N′).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 7G comparing different constructs.

claim: The Dia-N′ construct, in which the binding domains for both cues are intact, displayed apical enrichment values of approximately 7, clearly indicative of synergy between Rho1 and PI(4,5)P2 in promoting Dia apical localization.
source: However, the Dia-N′ construct, in which the binding domains for both cues are intact, displayed apical enrichment values of ≈7, clearly indicative of synergy between Rho1 and PI(4,5)P2 in promoting Dia apical localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements showing that the combined effect is greater than either cue alone.

claim: A partial apical localization bias of Dia by Rho1 binding is significantly enhanced by binding to PI(4,5)P2.
source: Taken together, we show that a partial apical localization bias of Dia by Rho1 binding is significantly enhanced by binding to PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This claim summarizes the synergistic relationship between Rho1 and PI(4,5)P2 in Dia localization.

claim: Tight apical localization of Dia is critical for the formation of polarized actin tracks, guiding apical movement of secretory vesicles that are associated with MyosinV motors.
source: This tight apical localization is critical for the formation of polarized actin tracks, guiding apical movement of secretory vesicles that are associated with MyosinV motors (Massarwa et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Apical recruitment of Dia is mediated by binding to two distinct elements, PI(4,5)P2 and Rho1.
source: We found that apical recruitment of Dia is mediated by binding to two distinct elements, PI(4,5)P2 and Rho1.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Synergism between PI(4,5)P2 and Rho1 ensures highly efficient apical localization of active Dia.
source: Further analysis suggests that synergism between these two partial signals ensures highly efficient apical localization of active Dia.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the quantitative analysis showing enhanced localization when both binding sites are intact.

claim: Over-expression of tagged Sktl resulted in both a massive increase in the levels of apical PI(4,5)P2 and accumulation of Sktl at the same domain.
source: Over-expression of tagged Sktl resulted in both a massive increase in the levels of apical PI(4,5)P2 (not shown), and accumulation of Sktl at the same domain.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations, though the PI(4,5)P2 increase data is not shown.

claim: A Sktl protein that is catalytically inactive was distributed uniformly when expressed in a similar manner.
source: In contrast, a Sktl protein that is catalytically inactive was distributed uniformly, when expressed in a similar manner (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 4.

claim: The signal targeting Sktl apically may be limited, and capable of providing only an initial bias, with the resulting enrichment of PI(4,5)P2 following the activity of Sktl leading to recruitment of additional Sktl molecules and amplification of the apical bias.
source: We assume that the signal targeting Sktl apically may be limited, and capable of providing only an initial bias. The resulting enrichment of PI(4,5)P2 following the activity of Sktl can lead to the recruitment of additional Sktl molecules and amplify this apical bias.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observation that active Sktl localizes apically while inactive Sktl does not.

claim: In the moss Physcomitrella patens, class-II formins bind PI(3,5)P2, leading to their cortical localization, and allowing them to mediate polarized growth.
source: In the moss Physcomitrella patens, class-II formins bind PI(3,5)P2, leading to their cortical localization, and allowing them to mediate polarized growth (van Gisbergen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phospholipids are emerging as important regulators of formin localization and activity at the tissue and organismal level.
source: Taken together, phospholipids are emerging as important regulators of formin localization and activity at the tissue and organismal level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the current study and cited work on formins in different organisms.

claim: The mammalian formins mDia1 and mDia2 bind phospholipids through a basic domain (BD), located at the extreme N-terminus, which regulates both activity and recruitment to membranes in cell culture models.
source: The mammalian formins mDia1 and mDia2 bind phospholipids through a basic domain (BD), located at the extreme N-terminus. This BD was shown to regulate both activity and recruitment to membranes in cell culture models (Ramalingam et al., 2010; Gorelik et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Drosophila Dia contains an N-terminal basic domain which is critical for apical localization and is likely to mediate the association with PI(4,5)P2 through electrostatic interactions with the acidic phospholipid.
source: Similar to the mammalian homologues, Drosophila Dia also contains an N-terminal basic domain which is critical for apical localization (Figure 6), and is likely to mediate the association with PI(4,5)P2 through electrostatic interactions with the acidic phospholipid.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the importance of the BD, and by inference from known properties of basic domain-phospholipid interactions.

claim: Electrostatic interactions between basic domains and acidic phospholipids are known to be weak, and are usually insufficient to stably associate proteins with the membrane under physiological conditions, requiring coupling to additional membrane-targeting motifs.
source: These interactions are known to be weak, and are usually insufficient to stably associate proteins with the membrane under physiological conditions, requiring coupling to additional membrane-targeting motifs (Mulgrew-Nesbitt et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: The Dia BD proved insufficient to direct apical targeting on its own.
source: Indeed, the Dia BD proved insufficient to direct apical targeting on its own (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Dia differs from plant formins, which commonly contain a structured PTEN domain for phospholipid binding that confers strong and more specific association, and is consequently sufficient for cortical localization without requirement for additional targeting factors.
source: In this respect, Dia differs from plant formins, which commonly contain a structured PTEN domain for phospholipid binding. This domain confers strong and more specific association, and is consequently sufficient for cortical localization, without requirement for additional targeting factors (van Gisbergen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and comparison with the current findings.

claim: The constitutively activated, open conformation of Dia was significantly more accessible to apical targeting, probably as a result of exposing the N-terminus more readily to apical-targeting factors.
source: The constitutively activated, open conformation of Dia was significantly more accessible to apical targeting (Figure 1), probably as a result of exposing the N-terminus more readily to apical-targeting factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Even high levels of the open conformation of Dia were efficiently targeted, indicating that the targeting machinery is in relative excess.
source: Interestingly, even high levels of the open conformation of Dia were efficiently targeted, indicating that the targeting machinery is in relative excess.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that overexpressed open Dia still localizes apically.

claim: The generation of the open Dia conformation is normally facilitated by binding to Rho1.
source: Normally, the generation of the open Dia conformation is facilitated by binding to Rho1 (Otomo et al., 2005; Rose et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: For some formin-family proteins, phosphorylation of residues adjacent to the DAD domain by a Rho1 effector, ROCK-1, is an essential element in the activation process.
source: In addition, for some formin-family proteins, phosphorylation of residues adjacent to the DAD domain by a Rho1 effector, ROCK-1, is an essential element in the activation process (Takeya et al., 2008; Staus et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It remains to be determined whether ROCK-1 also plays a role in activation of Dia in Drosophila tubular organs.
source: It remains to be determined whether ROCK-1 also plays a role in activation of Dia in Drosophila tubular organs.
evidence: This is a statement about what is unknown, representing a gap in knowledge.

claim: There are indications for apical enrichment of Rho1 protein in Drosophila tubular organs.
source: There are indications for apical enrichment of Rho1 protein in Drosophila tubular organs (Massarwa et al., 2009 and Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: The distribution of the activated form of Rho1 may be even more apically biased than total Rho1.
source: The distribution of the activated form of Rho1 may be even more apically biased.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the possible distribution of active Rho1.

claim: Rho1 requires different signals than Dia for its apical localization.
source: It appears, however, that Rho1 requires different signals than Dia for its apical localization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that manipulating PI(4,5)P2 levels affects Dia but not Rho1 localization.

claim: Alterations in the PI(4,5)P2 distribution, which resulted in dramatic effects on the localization of Dia, had only a marginal effect on the localization of Rho1.
source: Alterations in the PI(4,5)P2 distribution, which resulted in dramatic effects on the localization of Dia, had only a marginal effect on the localization of Rho1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dia localization depends on Rho1, but the localization of Rho1 is independent of Dia and the apical actin cables it forms, suggesting a hierarchy rather than a reinforcing feedback loop between the two proteins.
source: While Dia localization depends on Rho1, the localization of Rho1 is independent of Dia and the apical actin cables it forms (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting a hierarchy rather than a reinforcing feedback loop between the two proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference about the relationship between Dia and Rho1.

claim: One possibility is that apical Rho1 localization involves anchoring to Rho-GEFs, the specific guanine-exchange factors that activate Rho1, which were also shown to be enriched in apical membranes of Drosophila tubular organs.
source: One possibility is that apical Rho1 localization involves anchoring to Rho-GEFs, the specific guanine-exchange factors that activate Rho1, and were also shown to be enriched in apical membranes of Drosophila tubular organs (Massarwa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about a possible mechanism for Rho1 localization, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The tight apical localization of Dia is achieved by combining functionally distinct apical-biasing cues.
source: Our results demonstrate that the tight apical localization of Dia is achieved by combining functionally distinct apical-biasing cues.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Neither Rho1 nor PI(4,5)P2 is sufficient to efficiently recruit Dia apically on their own.
source: Neither Rho1 nor PI(4,5)P2 is sufficient to efficiently recruit Dia apically on their own.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that constructs lacking either binding site show reduced localization.

claim: Combining Rho1 and PI(4,5)P2 binding gives rise to dramatic apical localization of Dia, demonstrating a synergistic contribution.
source: Nevertheless, combining these two relatively weak interactions gives rise to dramatic apical localization of Dia, demonstrating a synergistic contribution (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 7.

claim: The cooperative contribution of multiple domains within the same protein to drive membrane targeting is termed 'Coincidence detection'.
source: The cooperative contribution of multiple domains within the same protein to drive membrane targeting is termed 'Coincidence detection' (Lemmon, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established terminology.

claim: Coincidence detection can be used to generate enhanced targeting specificity, as a multidomain protein will bind with high avidity exclusively to membranes that encompass both cues.
source: This mechanism for localization of a multidomain protein can be used to generate enhanced targeting specificity. While both Rho1 and PI(4,5)P2 may separately reside in other subcellular domains, Dia will bind with high avidity exclusively to the apical membrane that encompasses both cues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the concept of coincidence detection and the experimental observations.

claim: Binding to Rho1 alone was weak but nevertheless detectable.
source: Binding to Rho1 alone was weak but nevertheless detectable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing residual localization of constructs that can bind Rho1 but not PI(4,5)P2.

claim: Binding to PI(4,5)P2 alone was not capable of generating any apical localization bias, despite its marked contribution to apical recruitment in the presence of Rho1.
source: Conversely, binding to PI(4,5)P2 alone was not capable of generating any apical localization bias, despite its marked contribution to apical recruitment in the presence of Rho1 (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Binding to activated Rho1 may represent the more prevalent scenario for the initial interaction of Dia with the apical membrane.
source: Binding to activated Rho1 may represent the more prevalent scenario for the initial interaction of Dia with the apical membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the asymmetry between the two cues.

claim: Rho1 binding gives rise to an open conformation of Dia, which is more amenable to targeting, and provides physical proximity to the membrane.
source: This interaction will also give rise to an open conformation of Dia, which is more amenable to targeting, and will provide physical proximity to the membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known effects of Rho1 binding on Dia conformation and the experimental observations.

claim: Membrane proximity allows the interaction of Dia with PI(4,5)P2, which was not favored when the Dia protein was cytoplasmic, due to low affinity restrictions.
source: Membrane proximity can now allow the interaction of Dia with PI(4,5)P2, which was not favored when the Dia protein was cytoplasmic, due to low affinity restrictions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PI(4,5)P2 binding alone is insufficient but contributes when Rho1 is present.

claim: The Dia-PI(4,5)P2 interaction stabilizes association with the apical membrane, resulting in synergy in the combined action of Rho1 and PI(4,5)P2 in Dia apical localization.
source: The Dia-PI(4,5)P2 interaction stabilizes association with the apical membrane, resulting in synergy in the combined action of Rho1 and PI(4,5)P2 in Dia apical localization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations showing synergistic effects.

claim: Once in the vicinity of the apical membrane, Dia can shift dynamically among three states, being bound to each of the cues alone, or to both simultaneously, which can increase the effective levels of apical-targeting cues.
source: Once in the vicinity of the apical membrane, Dia can shift dynamically among three states, being bound to each of the cues alone, or to both simultaneously. This feature can increase the effective levels of apical-targeting cues, since they do not necessarily have to be used simultaneously at all times.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The activity of N-WASP, the activator of the ARP2/3 actin nucleation complex, was shown to be dependent on the synergistic binding of the Rho GTPase Cdc42 and of PI(4,5)P2 to distinct domains in the protein.
source: The activity of N-WASP, the activator of the ARP2/3 actin nucleation complex, was shown to be dependent on the synergistic binding of the Rho GTPase Cdc42 and of PI(4,5)P2 to distinct domains in the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: N-WASP binding to Cdc42 and PI(4,5)P2 is not reported to lead to targeting of the protein to distinct subcellular domains, but rather to localized activation.
source: However, this binding is not reported to lead to targeting of the protein to distinct subcellular domains, but rather to localized activation (Prehoda et al., 2000; Padrick and Rosen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: dia mRNA is apically localized by a mechanism that is distinct from the protein localization machinery, leading to localized translation of Dia protein at the apical membrane.
source: As previously noted, dia mRNA is also apically localized by a mechanism that is distinct from the protein localization machinery, leading to localized translation of Dia protein at the apical membrane (Massarwa et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A more restricted apical distribution of endogenous Dia was observed compared with the over-expressed protein, which is not localized at the RNA level.
source: Indeed, we observed a more restricted apical distribution of endogenous Dia compared with the over-expressed protein, which is not localized at the RNA level (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: A bias in the apical localization of Dia activators (Rho-GEFs and Rho1) may provide another level of refinement in Dia localization.
source: In addition, a bias in the apical localization of Dia activators (Rho-GEFs and Rho1) may provide another level of refinement.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about additional mechanisms that may contribute to Dia localization.

claim: The bias in Rho-GEFs may be influenced by apical PI(4,5)P2 levels, providing an additional layer of convergence between distinct signals.
source: Finally, the bias in Rho-GEFs may be influenced by apical PI(4,5)P2 levels, providing an additional layer of convergence between distinct signals (Murray et al., 2012; Viaud et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents a speculative connection.

claim: This general mechanism in Drosophila tubular organs is likely to extend to tubular tissues in the mammalian system.
source: It is likely that this general mechanism in Drosophila tubular organs extends to tubular tissues in the mammalian system.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the MDCK cyst data and known conservation of mechanisms.

claim: A collaboration between PI(4,5)P2 and a Rho-family GTPase in membrane recruitment of mammalian mDia2 was observed in a cell culture system.
source: A collaboration between PI(4,5)P2 and a Rho-family GTPase in membrane recruitment of mammalian mDia2 was observed in a cell culture system (Gorelik et al., 2011), and here we have demonstrated the capacity of PI(4,5)P2 to influence Dia targeting in mammalian MDCK cysts (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The link between activation and localization, as well as the identity of the critical domain for localization of formin family proteins, appear to be conserved.
source: Furthermore, the link between activation and localization, as well as the identity of the critical domain for localization of formin family proteins, appear to be conserved (Carramusa et al., 2007; Watanabe et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activated mDia1 is targeted to the apical membrane in the tubular epithelium of secretory acinar cells in the mouse pancreas.
source: In this context, we have recently examined the tubular epithelium of secretory acinar cells in the mouse pancreas, and shown that activated mDia1 is targeted to the apical membrane (Geron et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: The Dia apical-targeting machinery appears to be common to a variety of tubular tissues, regardless of their origin or physiological function.
source: Thus, the Dia apical-targeting machinery appears to be common to a variety of tubular tissues, regardless of their origin or physiological function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations in multiple Drosophila tissues and mammalian systems.

claim: This work uncovers a mechanism by which Dia is targeted to the apical membrane of tubular epithelia, thereby restricting actin cable formation, and consequently secretion, to a distinct membrane domain of these cells.
source: In conclusion, this work uncovers a mechanism by which Dia is targeted to the apical membrane of tubular epithelia, thereby restricting actin cable formation, and consequently secretion, to a distinct membrane domain of these cells.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main conclusion of the study.

claim: This localization mechanism is likely to be universal to tubular epithelia in a broad range of organisms.
source: This localization mechanism is likely to be universal to tubular epithelia in a broad range of organisms.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the conservation observed across Drosophila and mammalian systems.
